tagline: Limestone moves from hillsides into barns, fences and an abolitionist church
intro: The Native Stone Scenic Byway links 75 miles of Kansas highways with limestone as its recurring feature. Kansas Tourism presents the scenic byway as a journey through natural rock formations and the work of masons who built communities from local stone. Stone barns and roughhewn fences accompany limestone on the hillsides, while a K-177 overlook faces Konza Prairie. Konza lies within the Flint Hills’ unplowed tallgrass prairie, where limestone outcrops appear throughout the landscape.

Part of this road corridor has an older traveling story: K-4 roughly follows the Southwest Trail, which connected the Oregon Trail at Topeka with the Santa Fe Trail at Council Grove. Dover offered one of only two wagon fords on Mission Creek, and an inn grew at that crossing. The Sage Inn’s northern half dates to 1865; its southern half was added in 1878. Around 1900, the railroad went to Harveyville instead of Dover, and the inn and stagecoach station declined.

Travel west to east from I-70 south of Manhattan, taking K-177 north and K-18 east toward Wabaunsee. K-99 leads south through Alma to K-4, which continues past Lake Wabaunsee and Eskridge toward Dover. The route ends east of Dover at Glick Road.
notice: Look for local limestone in hillside formations, stone barns and roughhewn fences.

moments.title: Beecher Bible and Rifle Church
moments.text: Local limestone gives the Beecher Bible and Rifle Church its walls; its name comes from the conflict over slavery in Kansas. Henry Ward Beecher helped finance rifles for the New Haven emigrants who settled Wabaunsee. The weapons passed through pro-slavery territory in crates marked “Beecher’s Bibles.” Church member Robert Banks built the church with contrasting stone accents, completing it in 1862 after four years of construction. A wooden bell tower rises above the gabled roof; inside, the main space was divided into men’s and women’s sides. Metal stovepipes connect the perimeter wood stoves to a central brick chimney.
moments.notice: The limestone walls have contrasting stone accents beneath a gabled roof and wooden bell tower.

moments.title: Alma
moments.text: Alma’s downtown concentrates its architectural history along Missouri Street between Second and Fifth streets. The historic district includes 21 contributing buildings, among them commercial buildings, a post office and a fire station. The county seat moved here from Wabaunsee after the Civil War. Then, in 1887, the Chicago, Kansas and Nebraska Railway built its main line through Alma. That same year Joseph and Christena Brandt built a limestone hotel for travelers and railroad passengers. Its tall arched windows and pressed-metal cornice survive in the restored Brandt House. Its entrance faces Missouri Avenue from a downtown corner.

moments.title: Lake Wabaunsee
moments.text: Lake Wabaunsee began as a relief-work project in 1933, when the Kansas Emergency Relief Corporation established a camp here. The Works Progress Administration took over the digging in 1936 and completed construction in 1937; Eskridge purchased the lake. During World War II, Fort Riley established a branch prisoner-of-war camp at the lake, west of Eskridge. Kansas Tourism now identifies the lake on K-4 as one of the byway’s interpretive sites.
